b: Almost every Christian knows the word amen, and few know what it means. It comes straight from the Hebrew, through Greek and Latin, into nearly every language, and it is built on a root that means firm, reliable and trustworthy. The same root gives the Hebrew word emunah, which means faithfulness, steadiness or faith. Amen is the response of agreement. It means "that is certain," "it is so," or "let it be so."

In the Old Testament the people say "Amen" at solemn moments, such as when they agree to the curses of the covenant (Deuteronomy 27:15-26) or when they praise God at the end of a psalm. Giving the word as a response means taking the statement as one's own.

Jesus used the word in a way that was unusual. In the Gospels he often begins a saying with "Amen, I say to you." The Berean Standard Bible renders it "Truly, truly, I tell you." Other teachers might close a prayer with amen, but Jesus put it at the start of his own teaching, to stand behind what he said with his own authority. In Revelation he is even called "the Amen, the Faithful and True Witness" (Revelation 3:14).

The connection between faith and faithfulness is one worth noticing. Habakkuk 2:4 is usually translated, "the righteous will live by faith," but the word emunah can also mean faithfulness, steady trust that holds firm over time. For the Hebrews, to believe is not mainly to hold an opinion, but to rely on someone, to stand on solid ground. So when we say amen, we are saying that we are standing on what God has said, and are trusting that it will hold.

The Greek word charis is translated grace, and it sits close to the center of the New Testament. Its ordinary meaning in Greek was favor, kindness or a gift freely given, something done out of goodwill without payment. Related words give us the English charity, charisma and Eucharist, which means thanksgiving. It is also related to the Greek word for joy, chara, and for rejoicing, chairo, which suggests that grace brings delight.

In the world of the first century, a favor was the currency of society. Rich patrons gave gifts to dependents, who were expected to repay them with loyalty and praise, so gifts tied people into a web of obligation. Paul turns the picture upside down. God's grace is a gift with no strings of that kind, given to people who have nothing to offer. He says that people are "justified freely by His grace" (Romans 3:24). The word "freely" translates a Greek word meaning as a gift, without cost, and it is related to charis.

The apostle also stresses that grace is not only a one-time gift of forgiveness but the continuing power by which Christians live. When Paul asked God to remove a thorn in his flesh, God answered, "My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). Grace there is a strength that arrives when our own is gone. And Titus says that "the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone," and that it teaches us to renounce ungodliness.

Because of the way it appears at the opening and closing of nearly all of Paul's letters, grace is also a standard greeting in the New Testament, for "Grace and peace to you." The Greek greeting was chairein, "rejoice," and the Hebrew was shalom. Paul combines them, and in doing so says what the gospel is: grace and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

The word covenant, in Hebrew berit, is one of the keys to the whole Bible. A covenant was a binding agreement between two parties, with promises and obligations, sealed by an oath and often a ceremony. In the ancient Near East kings made covenants, usually called treaties, with the nations they ruled. Families and friends made covenants, and so did husbands and wives.

The Hebrew idiom for making a covenant was to "cut" one, and it comes from the ceremony of cutting animals in half. This explains one of the strangest scenes in Genesis. When God makes his covenant with Abram, Abram brings a heifer, a goat, a ram and birds, splits the animals down the middle and lays the halves opposite each other. After dark, a smoking firepot and a flaming torch pass between the pieces (Genesis 15:9-18). In the ancient world the parties to a covenant would walk between the halves, as if to say, "May this happen to me if I break my word." Here only God passes through, and Abram, who was in a deep sleep, does not. God is taking the whole obligation on himself.

The Old Testament speaks of several covenants: with Noah, with Abraham, with Israel at Sinai, with David. Each one adds to the story. The prophets looked forward to a new covenant in which God would write his law on people's hearts and forgive their sins (Jeremiah 31:31-34). At the Last Supper Jesus took the cup and said, "This cup is the new covenant in My blood" (Luke 22:20).

In English, the two parts of the Bible are called the Old and New Testaments, and the word testament is the Latin for covenant. The titles say what holds the whole Bible together: God binds himself to his people by promise.

The English word gospel comes from the Old English godspel, "good story," which translates the Greek euangelion, "good news." In the ancient world the word was used for announcements of public events: the news of a victory in battle, the accession of a king, the birth of an heir to the throne. A herald who brought such news was said to euangelizo, to proclaim good news.

A famous example is an inscription found at Priene, in what is now Turkey, from about 9 BC. It records a decision by the cities of Asia to start the new year on the birthday of the emperor Augustus, and calls his birth the beginning of "good news" for the world. He was hailed as savior, and the one who brought peace. The first Christians would have seen the same vocabulary around them. When they used it of Jesus, they were making a claim: the real king, the real savior, the real bringer of peace was not Caesar.

The Old Testament had prepared the way. Isaiah speaks of the herald who brings good news to Zion, "Your God reigns!" (Isaiah 52:7), and of one anointed to preach good news to the poor (Isaiah 61:1). When Jesus began to preach in Galilee, he announced, "The time is fulfilled," He said, "and the kingdom of God is near. Repent and believe in the gospel!" (Mark 1:15). And the angel told the shepherds, "I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people: Today in the city of David a Savior has been born to you. He is Christ the Lord!" (Luke 2:10-11).

Paul gives the content of the gospel in one summary: that Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). It is news and not advice: something that has happened, which we are invited to believe and to join.

Few Hebrew words are harder to put into English than hesed. It appears about 250 times in the Old Testament, and translators have rendered it as kindness, mercy, love, steadfast love and faithfulness. The Berean Standard Bible uses "loving devotion." The English word "lovingkindness," in older versions, was coined by Miles Coverdale in 1535 just to translate it.

The idea is covenant loyalty: a love that keeps its promises, shows up when it is needed, and stays when it would be easier to leave. It is not just a warm feeling. It is an action done for a person to whom you are bound. It describes what Ruth does for Naomi, when she follows her mother-in-law to an unknown land. Boaz says to Ruth that her hesed now is greater than before (Ruth 3:10). It describes Jonathan's loyalty to David.

Above all it describes what God is like. When God proclaimed his name to Moses, he said that he is "compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6). It is the Old Testament's favorite word for his character, and it was repeated again and again in Israel's worship. Psalm 136 has twenty-six verses, each ending with the same refrain: "His loving devotion endures forever."

What makes hesed so important is that it sets God's love apart from the fickle gods of the nations. God's love for Israel does not depend on her merit. It comes from his own commitment, and it is the ground of every hope that he will forgive. The prophet Hosea builds a whole book on it. In the New Testament, the same idea stands behind the word grace, and behind Paul's confidence that nothing can separate us from the love of God.

The Hebrew word for glory is kabod, and it comes from a verb that means "to be heavy." A person with kabod has weight, in the sense of significance, honor, reputation and substance. We say something similar when we talk about a person of weight or a heavyweight. When the Bible says that God is glorious, it means that he is weighty, impressive and worthy of the highest honor.

The word is used in two main ways. It describes God's character and reputation, as when the psalm says, "Ascribe to the LORD the glory due His name; worship the LORD in the splendor of His holiness" (Psalm 29:2). To give God glory is to acknowledge his worth, to honor him as he deserves. It also describes a visible manifestation of his presence, a radiant, overwhelming light or cloud. It filled the tabernacle when Moses finished building it, so that Moses could not go in, and it filled the temple. Ezekiel saw it leaving Jerusalem and later returning.

Isaiah heard the seraphim cry, "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts; all the earth is full of His glory" (Isaiah 6:3). It is a great statement, saying that God's weight and splendor are not confined to the temple but are in the whole creation. And the New Testament makes the claim that this glory has come to live among us. John says, "The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth" (John 1:14). The Greek word doxa, glory, had in ordinary Greek the sense of opinion or reputation, so it was modified by its use in the Greek Old Testament to translate kabod.
When Christians say "Glory to God," they are saying that he is the one who matters most.

John opens his Gospel with a word that was full of meaning to his readers: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). The Greek is logos, and it means "word" but also speech, reason, account and principle. It was a word with a long history.

For Greek philosophers, from Heraclitus onward, the logos was the rational principle that ordered the universe, and the Stoics saw it in everything. A Jewish thinker in Alexandria named Philo, a contemporary of Jesus, had used the term for the mediator between God and the world. But John's source is the Old Testament more than philosophy. In Hebrew, the word for word, davar, also means a thing or an event, since a word of God is an act. "By the word of the LORD the heavens were made" (Psalm 33:6). God said "Let there be light," and there was. God's word creates, rescues, guides and heals. And the Old Testament had begun to speak of Wisdom and the word almost as persons who were with God.

John takes all of this and says something that no philosopher had said. The Word was with God, he was God, and "The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us" (John 1:14). The agent of creation, the order of the cosmos, the self-expression of God, became a man whom John could touch and see. The eternal reason was a person, and could be known.

For a Greek reader, this would be an invitation to see that what philosophers had longed for was now seen in Jesus. For a Jewish reader, it would recall Genesis and the creating word. For both, it said that Jesus is not just a teacher of truth, but is the truth himself.

One of the earliest Christian confessions was just two words in Greek: Kyrios Iesous, "Jesus is Lord" (1 Corinthians 12:3). To understand the force of it we need to know what the word meant in the first-century world.

Kyrios was a common word that meant master, owner or sir. A slave called his owner kyrios. It was also a title of respect, which could be given to anyone of rank. By the first century it had also become a title for gods and rulers, and the Roman emperors were increasingly addressed as kyrios. Citizens could be asked to burn incense and say "Caesar is Lord," and for Christians that was an impossible confession.

But there is a deeper background. When Jewish scholars translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek, they rendered the name of God, YHWH, as Kyrios, since they did not pronounce it. Every time the Greek Old Testament says "the Lord," it is the name of God. When the New Testament applies the same word to Jesus, and uses Old Testament verses about YHWH for him, it is making a very strong claim. Paul says, "if you confess with your mouth, 'Jesus is Lord,' and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved" (Romans 10:9). And in the hymn in Philippians, God has given him "the name above all names," that every knee should bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Philippians 2:9-11).

To call Jesus Lord is both to worship him as God and to submit to him as master. It means he is the one who has the final claim on a life. And it was dangerous: many of the early martyrs died because they would not say "Caesar is Lord." The little confession said who really ruled the world.

It is often said that Greek had four words for love: storge for family affection, philia for friendship, eros for romantic desire, and agape for self-giving love. The scheme was popularized by C. S. Lewis in his book The Four Loves in 1960, and it is useful. But the New Testament's use is less tidy than the popular version suggests, and it is worth knowing the details.

Agape was a rare word in ordinary Greek, and it came into wide use in the Greek translation of the Old Testament, where it was used for God's love and for human love. The New Testament writers adopted it for the love that Christians are called to. It describes the love of God for the world in John 3:16, and the great hymn to love in 1 Corinthians 13. John says that "God is love" (1 John 4:8). Its main sense is a love that acts for the good of another, with no need of a return. It is shown in giving: "God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son."

The popular claim is that agape always means divine, unconditional love and that phileo is lesser. That is too neat. The New Testament uses the verb agapao for less admirable loves too: "men loved the darkness rather than the Light" (John 3:19), and Demas, "in his love of this world, has deserted me" (2 Timothy 4:10). John also uses phileo of the Father's love for the Son, and the two words are used interchangeably in other places, as in the conversation between Jesus and Peter in John 21.

The sense depends on the context. What makes the Bible's idea of love distinctive is not a special word, but the way it is described: it is patient, kind, not self-seeking, and it endures (1 Corinthians 13). As Paul says, "these three remain: faith, hope, and love; but the greatest of these is love."

When Christians say Jesus Christ, they often treat Christ like a last name. In fact it is a title. The Greek word Christos means "anointed," and it translates the Hebrew mashiach, from which we get the English word Messiah. In the Gospel of John, when Andrew finds his brother Simon, he says, "We have found the Messiah," which is translated Christ (John 1:41). The two words say the same thing, in two languages.

To anoint is to pour or smear oil on a person to set him apart for a task. In Israel three kinds of people were anointed: priests, prophets and kings. When Samuel poured oil on David's head, "the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward" (1 Samuel 16:13). Kings in particular came to be called "the LORD's anointed" (the mashiach of the LORD). So, in the psalm, the kings of the earth set themselves "against the LORD and against His Anointed One" (Psalm 2:2).

After the exile, with no king on David's throne, the hope grew of a coming anointed one, a descendant of David who would restore the kingdom, defeat Israel's enemies and bring peace. People held different expectations, some thinking of a warrior and some of a priest or teacher. When the Gospels call Jesus the Christ, they are saying that he is that promised king, though he did the job in a surprising way, through suffering.

The title became so closely attached to Jesus that in Antioch his followers were first called Christians, "Christ's people" (Acts 11:26). Calling someone Christ also fits the three roles of anointing. He is the prophet who speaks God's word, the priest who offers himself, and the king who reigns. The word reminds us that Jesus is the fulfillment of a long story and that he was sent for a purpose.
Two Hebrew words in particular are translated "soul" and "spirit," and they show how differently the Old Testament thinks about human beings from the way many people do today.

Nephesh is the word used when God breathed into the man he had formed and "the man became a living being" (Genesis 2:7). It is the same word used of animals, and it can be translated life, person, creature or self. Its root has to do with the throat, and the word is sometimes used for a person's appetite or desire. In Hebrew thought, a human being does not have a soul. He is a soul, a living whole. When David says, "Bless the LORD, O my soul" (Psalm 103:1), he is addressing his whole self, with everything that he is.

Ruach means wind, breath and spirit, and the Hebrew uses one word for all three. It is the wind that blew over the waters in Genesis 1. It is the breath that gives a person life. It is the Spirit of God who comes on judges, prophets and kings. In Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones, the word ruach comes up again and again: God says he will cause breath to enter the bones, and they will come to life, and "I will put breath within you so that you will come to life" (Ezekiel 37:5-6). The word for the Spirit and for breath is the same.

Jesus plays on the idea in his conversation with Nicodemus. "The wind blows where it wishes," he says, and the wind and the Spirit are the same word in Greek, pneuma, as in Hebrew. Understanding these words helps us see that the Bible does not split a person into a body to be discarded and a soul to be saved. It speaks of people as living wholes, and of God's Spirit as the breath that gives life.

The Greek word pistis, with its verb pisteuo, is one of the most important in the New Testament. It is usually translated faith, and also belief, trust and, in some places, faithfulness. The range is wide, and a lot of confusion arises when English readers hear faith only as a religious word for believing something without evidence.

In ordinary Greek, pistis meant trust, confidence and reliability. A person could have pistis in a friend, or be a person of pistis, someone trustworthy. The word implies a relationship. To have faith in someone means to rely on them, to put one's weight on them. It is the opposite of anxious self-reliance. That is why Hebrews can define it as "the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see" (Hebrews 11:1), and then give a whole chapter of examples in which faith is shown as action: Noah building an ark, Abraham leaving home, Moses leaving Egypt.

The Latin Bible used the word fides, which gave us the English faith and fidelity. In the Middle Ages, faith came to be understood by some as intellectual assent, agreement to the church's teaching. The Reformers brought out the older sense: personal trust in Christ, a resting of the heart on him, with knowledge and agreement as parts of it. That is why Luther said that faith is a "living, daring confidence in God's grace."

One difficult case is a phrase in Galatians 2:16 and elsewhere, pistis Christou. It can be translated "faith in Christ," as the Berean Standard Bible does, or "the faithfulness of Christ." Scholars have debated it for decades, and some translations give the second as an alternative in a footnote. Both ideas are biblical: we are saved by trusting Christ, who was himself faithful to the Father to the point of death.

In the Old Testament the Hebrew word go'el, usually translated redeemer, has a specific, practical meaning. A go'el was a close relative who had the duty to protect and restore a family member in trouble. The law spelled it out in several ways. If a poor Israelite sold his land, the go'el could buy it back. If one sold himself into slavery, the go'el could pay his freedom. If a man was murdered, the go'el could pursue justice. And in the book of Ruth the duty also reaches to marrying a widow so that her husband's family line is not lost.

The best-known example is Boaz in the book of Ruth. He was a near relative of Naomi's dead husband, and when Ruth asked him to spread his cloak over her, he agreed to act, and in a public meeting at the town gate he bought the family land and took Ruth as his wife (Ruth 4:1-10). The story is a picture of how the go'el works: someone with the means and the willingness steps in at his own cost.

The word becomes a title for God. Job, in his deepest distress, declares, "I know that my Redeemer lives, and in the end He will stand upon the earth" (Job 19:25). In Isaiah, God says again and again to Israel in exile, "Your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel" (Isaiah 41:14). He is the kinsman who will rescue his people from slavery, as he did from Egypt and would from Babylon.

The New Testament takes it further. Paul writes, "In Him we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses" (Ephesians 1:7). The Greek word is apolytrosis, from the market of slaves and captives, where a ransom was paid. To call Christ the Redeemer is to say that he is the relative who has the right and the will to buy us back, and that he paid the price himself.

When John the Baptist and then Jesus began to preach, their first word was "Repent." In Greek it is metanoeo, from meta, "after" or "change," and nous, "mind." The literal sense is "to change one's mind," to think differently afterward. It is more than feeling sorry. It describes a change in the way a person sees things, which leads to a change in how he lives.

Behind it, in the Hebrew Bible, stands the verb shuv, which means to turn, to return. It is a very physical word, used for turning around on a path and going back the way you came. The prophets used it constantly in their call to Israel: return to the LORD. Joel says, "return to the LORD your God" (Joel 2:13). It is the picture of the prodigal son, who "came to his senses" and set out for home, and found his father running to meet him (Luke 15). Repentance is a turning back to someone who is waiting.

Taken together, the two words describe the whole movement. The mind changes, and so the direction changes. Paul sums up his own preaching by saying that he declared that people "should repent and turn to God, performing deeds worthy of their repentance" (Acts 26:20). That includes turning from something and turning to someone, and it is shown in a changed life.

It also shows what repentance is not. It is not self-punishment or a long display of regret, and it is not a sort of payment that earns forgiveness. The sorrow of repentance is real, but its aim is a return. Jesus said that there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:7), and the Bible presents the call to repent not as a threat but as an invitation to come home.

The Hebrew words tsedeq and tsedaqah, usually translated righteousness, are some of the most important in the Bible, and they are a good example of how English can mislead. We tend to hear righteousness as a private matter of moral purity, and justice as a public matter of courts and laws. In Hebrew the two are closely joined. The same word family covers both, and often a translator has to decide which English word to use.

The root idea is conforming to a standard: being in right relationship, doing what is right in a relationship. A righteous person is one who does what is right by God and by his neighbor. That is why the prophets spoke of righteousness in terms of care for the poor, honest weights and measures, fair courts and welcoming the stranger. Amos's cry, "let justice roll on like a river, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream" (Amos 5:24), uses two words that are almost a pair, and it is not by chance that they come together. The psalm says that "The LORD loves righteousness and justice" (Psalm 33:5).

When the New Testament was written in Greek, the same cluster of ideas was carried by the dikaios family of words. The word dikaiosyne can be translated righteousness or justice, and the verb dikaioo, "to declare righteous," gives us justification. That is why the doctrine of justification is not only about our private standing, but also about God putting things right. When Paul writes that God's righteousness has been revealed in the gospel, he means that God has acted to make the world right, as he promised.

This breadth is a corrective. Biblical righteousness cannot be reduced to personal piety, and it cannot be reduced to social action. It is a right relationship with God that shows itself in right relationships with people.

The English word salvation translates Greek soteria and Hebrew words from the root yasha, which have the sense of rescue, deliverance, safety and health. In the Old Testament, to be saved is to be delivered from some danger: from an enemy, from slavery in Egypt, from drowning, from illness, from exile. The song of Moses at the Red Sea says, "The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation" (Exodus 15:2). Jacob, dying, cries out, "I await Your salvation, O LORD" (Genesis 49:18).

The New Testament inherits the word and widens it. Salvation includes rescue from the guilt and power of sin, from death, and finally from the whole fallen order. In the Gospels the related Greek verb sozo can mean either to save or to heal, which is why one translation says that a person's faith has saved them and another says it has healed them. It describes a rescue in the present, in the past and in the future, so the New Testament can say that believers have been saved, are being saved and will be saved.

The name of Jesus is in fact built on the idea. "Jesus" is the Greek form of the Hebrew Yeshua, or Joshua, which means "the LORD saves." The angel explains it to Joseph: "you are to give Him the name Jesus, because He will save His people from their sins" (Matthew 1:21). The name is a promise and a job description.

Peter takes up the point when he stands before the Jewish council and says of Jesus: "Salvation exists in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved" (Acts 4:12). It is an exclusive claim, and the church has always taken it as the center of the gospel. The Savior is a person, and his name means what he came to do.

The Hebrew word shalom is usually translated "peace," and it is the greeting in Israel to this day. But its range is much wider than the absence of war. The root idea is wholeness, completeness, the state of everything being as it should be. Shalom can mean health, safety, prosperity, harmony in relationships and well-being in every part of life.

The word appears in the great priestly blessing that Aaron and his sons were to speak over the people: "May the LORD bless you and keep you; may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace" (Numbers 6:24-26). The final word is shalom. It was the summing up of all the other blessings.

Shalom is more than a feeling inside a person. It is a social and even cosmic condition. When the exiles in Babylon are told to "seek the prosperity of the city" where they live (Jeremiah 29:7), the word translated prosperity is shalom. They were to work for the wholeness of their pagan neighbors, and in it they would find their own. One of the psalms pictures the ideal in a line of poetry: "Loving devotion and faithfulness have joined together; righteousness and peace have kissed" (Psalm 85:10).

When the Old Testament looks forward to the Messiah, it calls him the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6), and the New Testament shows him coming to reconcile people to God and one another. When Jesus said to his disciples after the resurrection, "Peace be with you," he was using the ordinary greeting, with an extraordinary weight. The shalom that the Bible promises is not escape from life, but life as God made it to be.
shalom.q: Where in your life is shalom, in the full sense of wholeness, most missing right now?

b: When English Bibles print LORD in small capital letters, they are marking a particular Hebrew name: YHWH, written with four consonants and called the Tetragrammaton, "four letters." It is God's personal name, and it appears about 6,800 times in the Old Testament, more than any other word for God. It is tied to the verb "to be." When Moses asks God what name to give the Israelites, God says, "I AM WHO I AM," and "I AM has sent me to you" (Exodus 3:14).

Out of reverence, Jews stopped pronouncing the name in the centuries before Christ, and said Adonai, "my Lord," in its place. The Hebrew was written without vowels, so the original pronunciation was gradually lost. Scholars today usually reconstruct it as Yahweh. The word Jehovah is a later hybrid, formed in the Middle Ages by putting the vowels of Adonai on the consonants of YHWH. When the Old Testament was translated into Greek, the name became Kyrios, "Lord," and the New Testament's confession "Jesus is Lord" echoes it.

The Bible also uses other titles. Elohim, a plural in form but used with a singular verb when it refers to the one God, is the general word for God, and the first word of the Bible after "in the beginning." El Elyon is "God Most High," the title used by Melchizedek (Genesis 14:18). El Shaddai is usually translated "God Almighty," as when God appears to Abram (Genesis 17:1), though its exact meaning is uncertain. Adonai means "Lord" or "Master."

Names for God were also made by joining YHWH with something he had done. Abraham called the place on the mountain "The LORD Will Provide" (Genesis 22:14). Gideon built an altar named "The LORD Is Peace" (Judges 6:24). Each reveals a facet of who God is: he provides, he heals, he gives peace.

The Bible was written in three languages. Most of the Old Testament is in Hebrew, the language of ancient Israel. A few parts are in Aramaic, a related language that became the common tongue of the Near East under the Assyrians and Persians: a stretch of Daniel (2:4 to 7:28), parts of Ezra (4:8 to 6:18 and 7:12 to 26), one verse in Jeremiah (10:11) and two words in Genesis (31:47). The whole New Testament is in Greek.

Hebrew is written from right to left, with twenty-two letters, all consonants. For the first thousand years of its use, readers supplied the vowels from memory, and the little dots and dashes that mark them were added by the Masoretes between about AD 500 and 1000. Its vocabulary is concrete, rich in verbs and images, and a Hebrew word often covers more ground than any one English word.

By the time of Jesus, most Jews in Galilee and Judea spoke Aramaic at home. A few of his actual words are preserved in the Gospels in that language, such as talitha koum (Jesus' words to a little girl, "get up"), ephphatha ("be opened"), abba ("father") and the cry from the cross, Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani. Many people also knew Greek, which had spread across the Mediterranean after Alexander the Great and was the common language of trade, government and culture. Paul, a Jew from the Greek-speaking city of Tarsus, could address a Roman commander in Greek and a Jerusalem crowd in Hebrew or Aramaic (Acts 21:37 to 22:2).

The New Testament was written in an everyday form of Greek, called Koine, "common." It was not the elevated Greek of the philosophers, but the language of letters, contracts and market stalls. This suited the message. The gospel was written for ordinary people, in the language they spoke. The next lessons look at key words in Hebrew and Greek, to show what can be gained from knowing the sense behind the English.
the-three-languages-of-the-bible.q: Which Bible word or phrase have you only ever met in English, and what might you be missing?

b: The first five books of the Bible are called the Torah in Hebrew, and in most English Bibles the word is translated "law." It is not a bad translation, but it is a narrow one. The Hebrew word torah comes from a verb meaning "to direct" or "to teach," and its basic meaning is instruction, or teaching. It is the word used for a parent's guidance to a child (Proverbs 1:8), and for a priest's ruling on a question, and for the whole body of God's teaching to his people.

That helps explain why the psalms speak of loving the Torah in a way that would seem odd for a legal code. The first psalm says of the blessed man, "his delight is in the Law of the LORD, and on His law he meditates day and night" (Psalm 1:2). "The Law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul" (Psalm 19:7). Psalm 119, the longest chapter in the Bible, is a hundred and seventy-six verses of praise to God's instruction: "Oh, how I love Your law! All day long it is my meditation" (Psalm 119:97). It is the voice of someone who sees God's teaching as a gift, a map for the good life, and not a burden.

The Torah is also more than commands. It includes the stories of creation, the patriarchs and the exodus. The laws come inside a narrative of God's rescue. It tells Israel who God is, who they are and how to live as his people. The five books of Moses were the heart of Jewish worship and education, and the early Christians read them as a witness to Christ.

When the Greek translators rendered torah as nomos, "law," the sense was narrowed in many readers' minds to rules and regulations. Recovering the older meaning helps in reading Paul, who sometimes uses "the law" for the Torah as a whole, and sometimes for the requirements that it contains.
